newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS-Indonesia floats rupiah, currency plunges.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Indonesia floats rupiah, currency plunges.

text.p: Indonesia floated the rupiah on Thursday, triggering a steep 100-point fall in the currency against the dollar and taking it deep into uncharted waters.
Bank Indonesia, the central bank, announced it was lifting the intervention band with immediate effect, abandoning the parameters under which the bank steps into the foreign exchange market.
"Theoretically, it's a free float," bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
"But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course," he said, in order to smoothen the period of adapting to the new move.
"You can also call it a managed float without a band."
The rupiah dived on the news by more than 100 points from an opening of 2,648/58 against the dollar.
In mid-afternoon, it was trading at 2,750/60 and appeared to have temporarily stabilised, dealers said.
The bank had last fixed the intervention band at 2,378/2,682 on Wednesday.
Indonesia becomes the latest Southeast Asian nation to succumb to the currency pressures which have been afflicting the region since early July.
On July 1, the rupiah was trading at around 2,430 per dollar although subsequent pressures pulled it to a record low of 2,665 on July 21 and to 2,682 on Wednesday.

Djiwandono said the Thai baht and the Philippine peso had been floated since speculative attacks on regional currencies began, while the Malaysian ringgit and the Singapore dollar were being traded without any pre-announced limits.
"We are a regional market now. We are moving together," Djiwandono said.
"In the last few weeks Indonesia is the only one which had a band. It's the only one defending the rupiah," he said, adding that maintaining that position would be increasingly difficult.
"We are adjusting to the new realities," he said. "The new reality in the ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) region is floating (currencies)."
Economists said the move was a positive one.
"It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," said Desmond Supple, regional currencies specialist at BZW Asia in Singapore.
"Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth."
He said it was not surprising that the rupiah had plunged on the announcement but added that there was scope for recovery later.

"We are going to see substantial over-shooting," Supple said. "But it (the announcement) lays the conditions for reversal of the rupiah in the long-term and bring it back to a semblance of fair value."
Some market-watchers said it was possible that after abandoning the intervention band, Indonesia could introduce some form of mild capital controls to limit the scope for speculation.
Both Malaysia and Singapore have adopted systems which prevent sizeable non-trade forward transactions.
But Djiwandono said there would be no move to introduce exchange controls on the rupiah.
"Why should we control?" he said when asked if there was a possibility of any such move."
